title: JavaScript this binding and Function object methods
concepts: How a call site determines this for ordinary functions
How strict and non-strict calls differ
How bind creates a bound function
What function names, lengths, and prototype properties reveal

inventory.title: this values and call-site binding modes
Function.prototype methods and function classification behavior

accuracyFacts: For an ordinary function, this is determined by the call form, not the function's definition location. A property reference call such as object.method() supplies the base object, including when the method was inherited; extracting the function and calling it loses that receiver.

Strict ordinary functions receive exactly the this argument, including undefined, null, and primitives. Non-strict ordinary functions replace undefined/null with the global this value and box primitives. ECMAScript modules and class code are strict; a script's top-level this is distinct from the receiver of a sloppy detached function call.

Arrow functions have lexical this and lexical new.target; call, apply, and bind cannot replace an arrow's this. A method defined with concise method syntax has a dynamic receiver and is not constructible.

call and apply immediately invoke a callable; apply converts an array-like argument object to an argument list and treats null or undefined as an empty list. They pass thisArg without pre-coercing it; the target's strictness determines ordinary-function coercion.

bind creates a bound function with a fixed receiver and leading arguments. If the target is already bound, its receiver cannot be replaced. If the bound target is constructible, the bound function can be constructed; construction ignores bound this but keeps bound arguments and instanceof delegates to the target.

new.target is undefined in ordinary calls and is the construction target in construction. Arrows do not create a new.target binding. super property access uses the method's home object for lookup while the call receiver remains the current this.

Function.prototype.toString returns available source text for user functions, but host source availability may be withheld; built-in and other callable representations are implementation-defined. It is not a safe serialization or evaluator.

Function.prototype[Symbol.hasInstance] is the default hook used by instanceof and performs ordinary instance checking; a custom hook can change the result. The built-in hook is non-writable and non-configurable.

Function.prototype has no own Symbol.toStringTag property. Object.prototype.toString uses an internal callable-object fallback tag of Function when no string Symbol.toStringTag override is present; that fallback is not a Function-specific symbol property.

Function length and name are descriptive metadata, not invocation constraints or stable semantic identity. Function instance length is non-writable, non-enumerable, configurable; name has the same descriptor flags.

Only constructible function objects have an own prototype property used as the initial prototype for constructed instances. Bound functions, arrows, and ordinary concise methods lack it. Function.prototype itself is callable but not constructible and has no own prototype property.

Function.prototype.arguments and caller are legacy poison-pill accessors in the standard initial Function.prototype; access throws. Non-strict plain functions may expose implementation-defined legacy behavior, so neither property is portable or suitable for stack inspection.
